newsitem.title: USA: Albright asserts leading role of State Department.
newsitem.headline: Albright asserts leading role of State Department.

text.p: Madeleine Albright, starting to make her mark as America's first female secretary of state, has indicated her wish to restore the State Department as the dominant voice, with the president, in U.S. foreign policy.
Over the last four years, many officials and experts say, the department's influence -- along with its budget -- has declined, or at least its voice has been muted.
Albright goes so far as to argue that America's ability to carry out diplomacy is in danger, because of draconian budget cuts and public ignorance about the State Department's role.
"It is not too much to say that upon successful American diplomacy depends the future of the world," she told a packed auditorium of State Department officials last week.

Although not without his accomplishments, former Secretary of State Warren Christopher was not seen as a very compelling figure on the local or world stage and he did not wield power very effectively within the adminstration or with Congress.

He was unable to keep Congress from making serious new cuts in foreign affairs funding and sometimes saw other agencies -- the White House, Pentagon, Commerce Department, CIA -- chip away at State Department perogatives.

He was a lackluster public speaker and early on in President Bill Clinton's first term, saw other officials, like Albright who was then U.N. ambassador, sometimes pushed forward to articulate the public case for U.S. foreign policy.

Albright, by her own description and others, is energetic, aggressive and an animated and riveting speaker. She also appears to have celebrity status. The number of journalists travelling with Christopher dwindled over four years, but scores of media organisations -- and big TV news stars -- are clamouring to go with Albright on her first overseas trip, an around-the-world extravaganza set for mid-February.
If there were any doubt things would be different with Albright in charge, she made her intentions clear last week after assuming her new job.
"The foreign policy of the United States is not made in a dozen different offices in a dozen different agencies scattered around town," she told State Department employees.
"It is made in the Oval Office, and it is made here at the State Department. That is our responsibility and we will exercise that responsibility," she added.

The comment was remarkably candid and a clear sign to other members of Clinton's second-term cabinet. State Department officials were enthusiastic about her broad vision and her interest in restoring their organisation's importance.
Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, who introduced her at the State Department event, encouraged the view of Albright as "a victory-minded and victory-prone general."

What prompted Albright's comment "was a feeling that in recent months and years there had been devolution of the primacy of Secretary of State (in the cabinet) in formulating and articulating foreign policy," one official told Reuters.

Many officials and experts viewed China policy as controlled more by the White House and trade officials; Japan as dominated by trade officials and the Pentagon; Africa and Northern Ireland as controlled by the White House.
Also, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, because of a bombing last year at a U.S. military barracks in Saudi Arabia, now has a strong hand in policy toward the kingdom.
Several officials said they did not expect Albright to encourage internal administration bickering as the president seems to prefer his foreign policy advisers to work as a team.

But she will try to reclaim the policymaking initiative by choosing strong aides, including Thomas Pickering, the most highly-accomplished career diplomat, as the department's number three official, and Stuart Eizenstat, an experienced political appointee, as undersecretary of state for economic affairs.

In addition, her insistence on including China on her first overseas trip makes her the first member of Clinton's new cabinet to visit Beijing, and indicates the strong role she plans to play in managing that critical relationship.

Helmut Sonnenfeldt, foreign policy expert with the Brookings Institution, said: "I think she wants to be a player. No question about it. To what end remains to be seen" because U.S. foreign and domestic policy are so intertwined.
